text: Greene received enough reinforcements—roughly 1,600 Virginia State Line infantry and militia rifle units—to recross his main force into North Carolina on 23 February 1781. Greene replicated his earlier Cowpens operational approach by splitting heavy and light troops (flying army), thereby confusing Cornwallis while reducing the demand for provisions and fodder in a single district. After several days of feinting and skirmishing, Cornwallis tried to trap Colonel Williams’s flying army near Wetzell’s Mill, where it was “posted carelessly at separate plantations for the convenience of subsisting.” Cornwallis dispatched Colonel Webster’s reinforced brigade of 1,200 troops: three infantry regiments, Tarleton’s Legion, and a company each of Guards light infantry and Ansbach jaegers (riflemen). Williams’s flying army consisted of Lee’s 2d Partisan Corps, Pickens’s South Carolina militia regiment, three North Carolina militia companies, and a battalion of Virginia riflemen—about 700 troops. With Tarleton’s Legion in the vanguard, Webster’s brigade marched from their camp early on 6 March 1781 to catch the Americans in their bedrolls. The British advance was concealed by fog, but Lee’s pickets detected the enemy movement and gave the alarm. Williams immediately deployed his light infantry and militia to delay Webster’s advance while the Continentals and dragoons took up firing positions on the far side of Reedy Fork Creek. Lee’s light infantry drove back the initial attack, buying time for the American light troops to wade the creek. Webster riposted by sending his light infantry to cross upstream, but they were blocked in turn

by Colonel Washington’s 3d Legionary Corps, which screened Williams’s withdrawal back to Greene’s bivouac site. Each side lost about thirty casualties, but Cornwallis’s troops had fumbled an opportunity to encircle and destroy many irreplaceable Continentals. Williams’s near destruction reinforced Greene’s caution, and the British found American security tighter than before. Greene did not publicly criticize Williams after the battle, but Pickens’s militiamen were incensed at Williams’s blunder and most deserted for home. Greene was compelled to release Pickens to regroup his militia in South Carolina to keep the local loyalists in check. The quick American reaction, however, reflected the progress made by Greene and his officers in improving the combat effectiveness of the force.
citation: Skinner, Harold Allen, Jr. The War in the Carolinas and Georgia, 1781–1782. U.S. Army Campaigns of the Revolutionary War, CMH Pub 71-52. Washington, D.C.: Center of Military History, United States Army, 2026.
title: The War in the Carolinas and Georgia
